passages.topic: What an observer must look at in a foundational classroom
passages.text: Evidence of diverse pedagogy (toy-based, activity-based, experiential). … Multilingual transactions observed. … Academic climate of the class (child-friendly, participatory). … Inclusivity: equal opportunity for CWSN, advanced and struggling learners. … Effective use of TLM, ICT, and locally available/recycled materials. … Feedback provided in an encouraging, child-friendly way. … Questions designed to assess competency and application (not only recall).

passages.topic: Feedback to teachers and follow-up on the next visit
passages.text: Give constructive feedback to teachers and encourage joyful, experiential methods. … Observe pedagogy, inclusivity, classroom climate, and resource use. … Provide feedback and suggest follow-up measures to HM/Principal. … Review improvement in the next inspection.

passages.topic: Oral language and phonological awareness activities
passages.text: Picture Talk: Show a picture and let children describe what they see. … Sound Clap: Clap for each syllable in a word … Rhyme Time: Match words with similar sounds … Initial Sound Hunt: Find classroom objects beginning with a given sound. … Flash & Say: Flash a letter card; children say the sound and a word with it. … Word Wall: Create a wall of frequently used words in class.

Shared Reading: Teacher reads big books aloud; children follow with finger. … Paired Reading: Two children read together, supporting each other. … Story Sequencing: Arrange story pictures in correct order. … Picture Description: Children write 1–2 sentences about a picture. … Journal Writing: Maintain a daily/weekly notebook of simple sentences.

passages.topic: Concrete materials before symbols in numeracy
passages.text: Provide children with everyday objects like sticks, beads, stones, bottle caps, or counters to practice counting, addition, subtraction, and grouping. … Begin with concrete experiences before moving to abstract symbols and equations. … Example Activity: Distribute 10 beads among 2 children and ask how many each one gets.

Link mathematical concepts with everyday life situations. … Pose real-life problems that encourage children to apply mathematical thinking. … Encourage multiple approaches and peer discussions. … Example Activity: If there are 15 pencils and 5 students, ask how many pencils each will get

passages.topic: Support for children who are behind
passages.text: Observe children during activities rather than formal testing only. … For children struggling in literacy – provide extra reading time, phonics support, and peer reading. … For children struggling in numeracy – use concrete objects, repeat practice, and give visual aids.

Phonological Awareness: This domain includes the competencies of word awareness, rhyme awareness, and awareness of sounds within words … Decoding: This domain includes competencies of print awareness, akshara knowledge and decoding, and word recognition … Reading Fluency: Refers to the ability to read a text with accuracy, speed (automaticity), expression (prosody), and comprehension

passages.topic: Role of the CRC: visits and on-site support
passages.text: Regular academic inspection visits to schools, … Providing training and on-site support to schools and teachers, … Ensuring introduction and sustenance of innovative pedagogies in schools

passages.topic: Role of the CRC: TLM, slow learners, app-based reporting
passages.text: Ensuring effective use of all TLM provided to schools … Ensuring individualized support for CWSN and slow learners, … The reporting by CRC/BRC should preferably be App based, hence States/UTs may prepare Apps for reporting in the local language.

passages.topic: NIPUN Lakshyas for Class I and Class II
passages.text: Reads small sentences consisting of at least 4-5 simple words in an age appropriate unknown text. … Reads age appropriate unknown text of 8-10 sentences with simple words with appropriate speed (approximately 45to 60 words per minute correctly) comprehension, and clarity.
Reads atleast60 words per minute correctly and with comprehension … Solves daily life problems using addition and subtraction of numbers up to 999, sum not exceeding 999

passages.topic: What early language classrooms usually look like
passages.text: At present, early language classrooms are focussed mainly on teaching the varnamala and ma- tras, choral repetition of a text being read by the Teacher or children and copying or handwriting practice. There is little emphasis on meaning-oriented work, and few opportunities are provided for children to develop as readers and writers.

Creating a print-rich environment in the classroom through use of print resources (e.g., big books, picture books, story posters, poem posters, children’s magazines) displayed or kept in the classroom within children’s reach. … Setting up a ‘reading corner’ and ‘writing corner’ in the classroom.

Decoding instruction should follow activities of phonological awareness, where attention needs to be directed to sounds in words (beginning, middle, ending sounds). … Explicit instruction needs to be given for word decoding and spelling with segmenting and blending words and aksharas.

The intent is not for the children to repeat after the Teacher but to develop their language capacities and vocabulary. … In guided reading, the responsibility for reading shifts from the Teacher to the children. … Children must be given opportunities to read independently or with a partner.

passages.topic: Modelled and shared writing instead of copying
passages.text: copywriting is not a very meaningful activity for children, even if it helps in developing writing fluency. … For example, they can start a sentence “I ate ___ for breakfast” on the board and ask a child to come and complete it.
The language used by the Teacher should be simple and supported by gestures, pictures, actions, and use of words from the children’s home languages. … Create a stress-free and safe environment.

reasoning i.e., justifying and reasoning about solutions and processes; connec- tion-making i.e., connections between one concept and another; representation i.e., using con- crete, visual diagrams to represent mathematical concepts and ideas; communication i.e., ex- plaining and communicating mathematical ideas

E – Experience: Learning the mathematical concept of concrete objects, e.g., counting … L – Spoken Language: Describing the experience in language … P – Pictures: Representing mathematical concepts in a pictorial form … S – Written Symbols:
Learning mathematics must relate to children’s real life and their prior knowledge. … Teachers should use real life examples to build conceptual and problem-solving abilities.
